subject: chemistry
title: Reactivity of metals
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Reactivity of metals — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.4.1.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Reactivity of metals, specification section 4.4.1.
final_note: You worked through Reactivity of metals — 21 specification statements.

concepts.def: A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. When a metal reacts with oxygen the metal gains oxygen, so the metal is oxidised.
A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen. When a metal oxide is heated with carbon the oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced.
The compound formed when a metal reacts with oxygen, for example magnesium oxide from magnesium burning in air.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together: oxygen lost by one substance is gained by another.
A list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity, deduced from their reactions with water and with dilute acids.
The readiness with which a metal atom loses its outer electrons to become a positive ion. The greater this tendency, the more reactive the metal.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound.

concepts.term: Carbon and hydrogen in the series
concepts.def: The two non-metals often included in the reactivity series as reference points; carbon sits between magnesium and zinc, hydrogen between iron and copper.

concepts.term: Reaction of a metal with water
concepts.def: A reaction at room temperature giving a metal hydroxide and hydrogen, shown by potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium, and only very slowly by magnesium.

concepts.term: Reaction of a metal with dilute acid
concepts.def: A reaction giving a salt and hydrogen, shown by magnesium, zinc and iron; copper does not react with dilute acid.
A metal found in the Earth as the element itself rather than as a compound, because it is very unreactive; gold is the standard example.
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile.
Heating the oxide of a metal that is less reactive than carbon with carbon, so that the carbon takes the oxygen and the metal is left.
The loss of electrons by a species during a reaction.
The gain of electrons by a species during a reaction.
An equation showing only the species that change in a reaction, with spectator ions left out.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, for example Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.
An ion present in the reaction mixture that is unchanged by the reaction and is therefore omitted from the ionic equation.

mcqs.q: Magnesium ribbon is burned in air and a white powder is left behind. Which statement about the magnesium is correct?
options: The magnesium gains oxygen, so the magnesium is oxidised.
The magnesium gains oxygen, so it has been reduced.
The magnesium and the oxygen are simply mixed.
The magnesium is used up, so it must be reduced.
mcqs.explain: Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides, and the reaction is an oxidation because the metal gains oxygen.

mcqs.q: Copper is heated in air and a black solid forms on the surface. What is the black solid and what has happened to the copper?
options: Copper oxide, though this is not an oxidation.
Copper oxide; the copper has been oxidised.
A mixture of copper and air joined on.
Copper oxide; the copper has been reduced.
mcqs.explain: Copper reacts with oxygen to give copper oxide, and gaining oxygen is oxidation, however gently the reaction proceeds.

mcqs.q: In the reaction 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, which substance is reduced, and why?
options: Carbon, because it gains oxygen in this.
Copper oxide, because the mass falls.
Copper oxide, because it loses oxygen.
Carbon, since it removes the oxygen atoms.
mcqs.explain: Reduction in terms of oxygen is loss of oxygen; the copper oxide gives up its oxygen to the carbon.

mcqs.q: Which statement about oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen is correct?
options: Reduction is gain of oxygen; oxidation is loss of it.
Reduction means the mass of the solid gets smaller.
A reaction shows oxidation or reduction, never both.
Oxidation is gain of oxygen; reduction is loss.
mcqs.explain: This is the definition required by the specification: reduction and oxidation explained in terms of loss or gain of oxygen.

mcqs.q: A metal reacts with another substance. What happens to the metal atoms during the reaction?
options: The metal atoms lose electrons and form positive ions.
The metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.
The metal atoms gain protons and become positive.
The metal atoms stay neutral and just join on.
mcqs.explain: When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions by losing their outer electrons.

mcqs.q: The reactivity of a metal is related to which property of its atoms?
options: Its tendency to grip its own electrons.
Its tendency to form positive ions.
How dense and hard the metal is.
The ability to form negative ions.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions.

mcqs.q: From their reactions with water and with dilute acids, which metal is placed highest in the reactivity series?
options: Copper, as it will not react with dilute acid.
Calcium, since it loses two electrons per atom.
Potassium, as it reacts fast with cold water.
Zinc, since its atoms have most mass.
mcqs.explain: Potassium reacts most vigorously of all these metals with cold water, so it stands at the top of the order.

mcqs.q: The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series. Why?
options: They are included because they are unusual metals.
They are placed there because every ore holds carbon.
They show that carbon extracts any metal from its ore.
They are reference points to compare metals with.
mcqs.explain: Including them lets a metal be judged as above or below carbon or hydrogen, which is what predicts extraction and acid reactions.

mcqs.q: A strip of magnesium is left in copper(II) sulfate solution. A pink-brown solid forms on the strip and the blue colour fades. Why?
options: Magnesium is more reactive, so it displaces the copper.
Copper is more reactive, so it displaces magnesium.
Both are metals, so they simply swap places.
The blue fades because the solution was diluted.
mcqs.explain: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound, so magnesium takes the place of copper and copper metal is deposited.

mcqs.q: Which mixture will produce a displacement reaction?
options: Copper added to zinc sulfate solution.
Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
Iron added to magnesium sulfate solution.
Copper added to iron(III) sulfate solution.
mcqs.explain: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so zinc displaces copper from the solution.

mcqs.q: Which metal reacts with cold water at room temperature to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen?
options: Zinc, which bubbles steadily in cold water.
Copper, used in pipes that carry water.
Sodium, which fizzes on the water surface.
Iron, because it rusts whenever it gets wet.
mcqs.explain: Sodium is above magnesium in the reactivity series and reacts readily with cold water to give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

mcqs.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. What are the products?
options: Magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas.
Magnesium chloride and water only.
Magnesium chloride and chlorine gas.
Magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
mcqs.explain: A metal reacting with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen; with hydrochloric acid the salt is the chloride.

mcqs.q: A piece of copper is left in dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Which statement describes what happens?
options: Nothing happens, because copper is below hydrogen.
It fizzes steadily and gives off hydrogen.
It reacts, but too slowly for bubbles to show.
It dissolves slowly and turns the acid blue.
mcqs.explain: Copper is the least reactive metal in the list and lies below hydrogen, so it does not displace hydrogen from a dilute acid.

mcqs.q: Potassium reacts far more vigorously with cold water than magnesium does. What best explains this difference?
options: Potassium holds on to its electrons more strongly.
Potassium loses its outer electron more readily.
Potassium loses two electrons, magnesium one.
Potassium is a softer, less dense metal.
mcqs.explain: Reactivity is related to the tendency to form positive ions, and potassium gives up its outer electron much more easily than magnesium.

mcqs.q: Metals X and Y are added to dilute acid. X fizzes vigorously while Y fizzes only slowly. What does this show about the atoms?
options: Y gives up its outer electrons more easily than X.
X can form negative ions more readily than Y.
X forms positive ions more readily than Y.
X has more electrons in total than Y has.
mcqs.explain: The vigour of the reaction with dilute acid reflects how readily the metal atoms give up electrons to form positive ions.

mcqs.q: Four metals are added to dilute acid. P bubbles very fast, S bubbles moderately, Q bubbles slowly and R shows no change. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
options: R, Q, S, P - slowest bubbling means most reactive.
R, P, S, Q - no reaction at all means most reactive.
P, S, Q only - R cannot be placed in the series.
P, S, Q, R - fastest bubbling is most reactive.
mcqs.explain: Rate of reaction with the same dilute acid ranks the metals directly, and a metal showing no change is the least reactive of the set.

mcqs.q: In separate tests, metal A displaces metal B from its sulfate solution, and metal B displaces metal C from its sulfate solution. What can be concluded?
options: A is the most reactive of the three and C the least.
C is the most reactive and A the least reactive.
A and B are ordered, but C cannot be placed.
All three are equally reactive as all reacted.
mcqs.explain: The two results chain together into one order, A above B above C, which is exactly how an order of reactivity is deduced from results.

mcqs.q: Gold is found in the Earth as the metal itself rather than as a compound. Why?
options: Gold was reduced by carbon deep underground long ago.
Gold is unreactive, so it does not form compounds.
Gold is very rare, so too little of it can react.
Gold is so dense that it sinks below the ores.
mcqs.explain: Unreactive metals such as gold are found as the metal itself; most other metals are found as compounds needing chemical extraction.

mcqs.q: Iron oxide is heated with carbon and iron metal is obtained. Why does this method work for iron?
options: Iron is more reactive than the carbon.
Carbon reduces every metal oxide.
Iron is less reactive than carbon.
The carbon melts the iron out of the ore.
mcqs.explain: Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.

mcqs.q: Which metal cannot be extracted from its oxide by reduction with carbon?
options: Copper, which is well below carbon.
Zinc, since carbon cannot reduce it.
Iron, whose ore must be melted first.
Potassium, which is above carbon.
mcqs.explain: Potassium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from potassium oxide.

mcqs.q: What does the term reduction mean when a metal is obtained from its oxide?
options: The oxide loses its oxygen and metal is left behind.
The oxide gains extra oxygen from the carbon.
The mass of the solid in the furnace falls.
The oxide melts and the metal simply runs out.
mcqs.explain: Reduction involves the loss of oxygen, which is exactly what happens to the oxide during extraction.

mcqs.q: A furnace is charged with lead(II) oxide and carbon. The reaction is 2PbO + C -> 2Pb + CO2. Which statement about this process is correct?
options: Lead lies above carbon in the reactivity series.
Lead is below carbon in the reactivity series.
Carbon is reduced and lead oxide is oxidised.
Only reduction occurs; nothing is oxidised.
mcqs.explain: Carbon has taken the oxygen from the lead oxide, which can only happen if lead is less reactive than carbon.

mcqs.q: A student is told that a metal M is found in the Earth as its oxide and that M is obtained by heating that oxide with carbon. What can be deduced about M?
options: M must be more reactive than carbon.
M is just as unreactive as gold.
M is less reactive than carbon is.
M's reactivity does not matter at all.
mcqs.explain: Only a metal below carbon can have its oxygen taken by carbon, so the stated method places M below carbon.

mcqs.q: In the reaction 2Fe2O3 + 3C -> 4Fe + 3CO2, which substance is oxidised?
options: Carbon, because it loses oxygen here.
Iron oxide, because it gains oxygen.
Iron oxide, because it loses its oxygen.
Carbon, because it gains oxygen.
mcqs.explain: The carbon gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide, and gain of oxygen is oxidation.

mcqs.q: In terms of electrons, which statement is correct?
options: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain.
Oxidation is the gain of electrons and reduction the loss.
Oxidation is the loss of protons and reduction the gain.
Oxidation and reduction both involve losing electrons.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition of oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons.

mcqs.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, which species is oxidised and why?
options: Zinc, since it gains two electrons.
Zinc, because it loses its two electrons.
The copper ion, because it loses electrons.
The copper ion, as it becomes a metal.
mcqs.explain: Zn becomes Zn2+, a loss of two electrons, and oxidation is the loss of electrons.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which is the correct ionic equation?
options: Mg + CuSO4 -> MgSO4 + Cu
2Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu
Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu
Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg+ + Cu
mcqs.explain: Only the species that change are shown; magnesium loses two electrons and the copper ion gains them.

mcqs.q: Which half equation shows a species being reduced?
options: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-, a gain of two electrons.
Mg + 2e- -> Mg2+, electrons are taken in.
Cu2+ -> Cu + 2e-, showing a gain of two.
Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, a gain of electrons.
mcqs.explain: Electrons appear on the left and are taken in by the ion, and gain of electrons is reduction.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.4.1 Reactivity of metals
